docs.title: 🧠 Introduction
docs.text:
Welcome — this is a living showcase of the projects I’ve been building lately....

To be brutally honest, every single one of these projects was coded by AI. I’ve been experimenting with tools like Kiro.dev, OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, and Google Gemini — but mostly Kiro.

The last time I personally wrote code was back in the 1990s... and let’s be real — nobody’s hiring for Turbo Pascal anymore.

docs.title: 🧪 The Experiment
docs.text:
When Kiro launched in Preview (June 2025), I was lucky enough to get early access. Since then, I’ve been running a series of small, two-to-three-week micro-hackathons, exploring what’s possible when you combine: - 🧩 AI-generated code - 🧠 Some level of Human architectural thinking - 🧾 Spec-driven development - 🎛️ Rapid iteration and design feedback

These projects represent that ongoing journey — blending AI’s speed with human intent. They are not production ready or final versions, more like prototypes that might be of interest.

Most of the content, like this doucmentation and the demostrations have most been done vai AI.

docs.title: Ambient Banking Assistant — AI-Native Financial Copilot Demo
docs.text:
TL;DR: A strategic product demo that shows what banking could feel like in 2028. Natural language replaces app navigation — the AI understands intent, reasons over financial context, applies policy guardrails, and executes safe banking actions. Designed to land with stakeholders in under 3 minutes.

Stack: React 19 • Vite • Framer Motion • Client-side only (no backend, no API keys)

docs.title: ✨ Features
docs.text:
• 📱 Ambient Entry - iPhone home screen with Apple Intelligence rainbow border; Siri query flows directly into the banking session
  • 🔐 Biometric Auth - Face ID scan animation before the banking app is revealed
  • 💬 Natural Language Banking - Intent engine parses queries like "Can I afford a £900 holiday?" into structured actions with full reasoning traces
  • 🛡️ Policy Engine - Transfer rules enforced visually (min balance £1,000; confirmation required above £500); policy outcomes shown inline
  • 🧠 Reasoning Drawer - Expandable AI trace panel showing intent confidence, reasoning steps, financial calculations, and policy outcome — makes it feel like a real AI system, not a UI mock
  • 📊 Structured UI Cards - Every assistant response renders rich inline cards: breakdown tables, animated bar charts, action buttons
  • ⚡ 2028 / Future Mode - Toggle frictionless mode: transfers execute without confirmation, reasoning shows "friction waived" language, continuous biometric session narrative
  • 🎛️ Presenter Controls - Play/pause autopilot, prev/next scene, scene jump, reset, dark/light theme toggle

docs.title: 🎬 Demo Flow
docs.text: Scene Name What Happens 0 Ambient Entry iPhone home screen + Apple Intelligence glow; user types query to Siri — Biometric Auth Face ID animation; in 2028 mode the Siri query passes through automatically 1 Financial Awareness "How much money can I spend this month?" → Monthly breakdown card with Safe-to-Spend figure 2 Spending Insight "Where does my money go each month?" → Category analysis with animated bar chart 3 Affordability Reasoning "Can I afford a £900 holiday?" → Budget impact, savings goal delay, AI reasoning trace 4 Safe Transfer "Move £600 from savings to current" → Policy engine fires, approval confirmation required 5 Behavioural Intelligence Proactive insight card — 3-month restaurant spend trend (Jan £265 → Feb £298 → Mar £420) 6 Intelligent Support Multi-step: unknown charge → dispute → merchant block → human specialist handoff 7 Platform Overlay Architecture stack + business value metrics for decision-makers

    Presenter[🎛️ Presenter Controls] -->|DOM events| App[App.jsx\nDemo Lifecycle]
    App -->|showHomeScreen / showAuthScreen| Intro[HomeScreenIntro\nBiometricAuthScreen]
    App -->|demoPhase / futureMode| Panel[ConversationPanel.jsx\nChat UI + Autopilot]

    Panel -->|user message| Intent[intentEngine.js\nRegex NLU → intent + params]
    Intent --> Policy[policyEngine.js\nTransfer rules validation]
    Policy --> Handler[Intent Handler\nbuilds trace + UI card]

    Handler --> Context[BankingContext.jsx\nGlobal state + mock operations]
    Handler --> Drawer[ReasoningDrawer.jsx\nAI trace panel]
    Handler --> Card[Inline React Card\nbreakdown / chart / buttons]

    App -->|showPlatformOverlay| Overlay[PlatformOverlay.jsx\nArchitecture + business value]

    subgraph "Data Layer (client-side only)"
        Context --> MockData[mockData.js\nSingle source of truth\nbalances · expenses · income · goals]

docs.title: No Backend, Full Credibility
docs.text: Every chart, reasoning trace, policy check, and insight card is deterministic and pre-authored in mockData.js. There are no live LLM calls, no API keys, no environment variables. The demo runs entirely in the browser — it can be deployed as a static site and presented anywhere with zero infrastructure risk.

docs.title: Policy as a First-Class UI Concern
docs.text: The transfer flow surfaces policy outcomes visually: CheckCircle / AlertTriangle icons with explicit policy reason text ("Transfer exceeds confirmation threshold", "Minimum balance maintained"). This turns a backend rule into a trust signal that stakeholders can see and understand.

docs.title: Reasoning Drawer — The "AI" Feel Without the AI
docs.text: The ReasoningDrawer anchored to the left of the phone frame shows a structured trace object: intent confidence score, step-by-step reasoning, financial calculations, and policy outcome. In 2028 mode it adds futureNote fields explaining the contrast. This single component is what makes the demo feel like a real AI system rather than a click-through prototype.

docs.title: Presenter-Friendly Autopilot
docs.text: The control bar at the bottom drives an async autopilot loop with realistic typing delays. Scene skipping works by throwing a 'Skip' error inside a wait() helper — the presenter can jump to any scene mid-flow without state corruption.

docs.title: State & Event Architecture
docs.text:
• All banking state lives in BankingContext.jsx — balances, expenses, operations — consumed via React context
  • App.jsx ↔ ConversationPanel.jsx communication uses a custom DOM event bus (START_AUTOPILOT_DEMO, RESET_CHAT, AUTOPILOT_CTRL, DEMO_PHASE_UPDATE) — deliberately decoupled so either side can be replaced independently
  • demoCore ref ({ active, playing, skip, target }) drives the autopilot loop without triggering re-renders

docs.title: Intent + Policy Pipeline
docs.text:
• intentEngine.js — regex-based NLU extracts intent and parameters from free-text input
  • policyEngine.js — stateless rule evaluator: minimum balance £1,000, confirmation threshold £500; returns { status, reason } used directly in UI card rendering

docs.title: Styling & Animation
docs.text:
• iOS device frame (390×844px) in pure CSS with Dynamic Island pseudo-element
  • Framer Motion throughout for all interactive transitions
  • Full light/dark theme via CSS custom properties on the root element; brand colours: --brand-blue: #00395D, --brand-cyan: #00AEEF

docs.title: 📊 Key Metrics
docs.text:
• Demo length: 8 scenes completable in under 3 minutes (autopilot)
  • Infrastructure: Zero — fully static, no backend, no API keys
  • Single source of truth: All financial figures in one file (mockData.js) — change once, propagates everywhere
  • ESLint: Flat config (ESLint 9+), no suppressions

This project demonstrates how deterministic, presenter-friendly demos can create genuine stakeholder conviction — and how thoughtful UI design (policy indicators, reasoning traces, structured cards) can make a no-backend prototype feel like production AI.

docs.title: Beat Your Mates — Always-On Prediction Agent
docs.text:
TL;DR: A spec-driven prediction agent for Sky Super 6 and Last Man Standing. A frozen, weighted Dixon-Coles model turns historical results into score matrices and expected-value picks, blended with bookmaker odds. The agent recommends and the human enters the picks, because it has no way to submit anything to Sky.

Stack: Python 3.12 • uv • numpy/scipy/pandas • PuLP • SQLite • stdlib http.server + vanilla JS UI • Docker Compose • macOS LaunchAgent

docs.title: ✨ Features
docs.text:
• ⚽ Quantitative core - Historical results feed a weighted Dixon-Coles model, then a score matrix, then Super 6 expected value, giving six recommendations plus a Golden Goal pick
  • 🧪 Walk-forward backtesting - Every model change is compared against baselines on held-out seasons, with ablation scripts for Elo, market, shot-proxy and totals variants
  • 🎯 Last Man Standing mode - Picks stay provisional until kickoff, and the dashboard previews every eligible club for each entrant
  • 📈 Market and availability layers - The Odds API consensus (20 UK books), football-data.org results and Tavily news run as separately scheduled jobs
  • 🕒 Restart-safe scheduler - SQLite-backed jobs of three types (POLL_ODDS, POLL_AVAILABILITY, KNOWLEDGE_RESEARCH) polled by bym tick
  • 🖥️ Local decision UI - Home, Round, Cup Match, League, Opponents, Performance, Activity and an Expert group (Model Lab, Sources, System Health, Settings)
  • 🏆 Season simulation - Monte Carlo season simulator labels rounds ATTACK, DEFEND or NORMAL against private-league opponents
  • 🔁 Self-healing service - A macOS LaunchAgent runs at login and re-runs start every 300 seconds
  • 🔭 Fantasy Premier League - A 29-module fpl/ package covers harvest, projection, lineup and transfer optimisation, with its own 1,636-line spec

docs.title: 🧠 Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Src[Football-Data.co.uk<br/>E0 + E1] --> Fetch[bym fetch<br/>cached forever when complete]
    Fetch --> Model[Weighted Dixon-Coles<br/>FROZEN_PHASE1_V1]
    Odds[The Odds API<br/>consensus] --> Model
    Model --> Matrix[Score matrix<br/>once per gameweek]
    Matrix --> EV[Super 6 EV + LMS outlooks]
    EV --> UI[Local web UI :8000]
    Worker[bym tick worker] --> DB[(data/bym.db)]
    UI --> DB
    Reg[Source registry<br/>APPROVED only] -.gates.-> Fetch
    Reg -.gates.-> Odds
    UI -->|recommendation only| Human[Human enters picks on Sky]

Seasons are assigned fixed roles by docs/VALIDATION.md:

flowchart LR
    T["2019/20 to 2023/24<br/>Training"] --> H["2024/25<br/>Hyperparameter validation"]
    H --> F{{"Freeze model"}}
    F --> X["2025/26<br/>Single-use holdout"]

docs.title: Rules enforced by tests, not by convention
docs.text: Each rule has a test or gate behind it, because breaking it silently invalidates a result. FROZEN_PHASE1_V1 writes every parameter out literally (xi=0.003, market_blend_weight=0.5, refit_every_days=7), so any change shows up as a diff in review. A failing test means the freeze was violated. The prospective 2026/27 comparison depends on this: if the constant drifted, the new agent would be compared against itself.

docs.title: A holdout that can only be spent once
docs.text: assert_holdout_unspent raises HoldoutAlreadySpentError whenever results/final_test_<season>.md already exists. No flag or caller can override it. It was added after a logged protocol breach on 2026-08-08, when a holdout was re-run and compared again. The existing result file is the record, and a new holdout needs a new season.

docs.title: Source gating and the Sky boundary
docs.text: The registry in sources/registry.py refuses queries to any source that isn't APPROVED. Promotion from REVIEW_REQUIRED is a deliberate human act, and PROHIBITED sources cannot be promoted. Sky Sports Super 6 is marked permanently prohibited, so fixtures and deadlines are entered by hand and no submission path exists. The agent sits outside Sky by design: it recommends, and the human submits.

docs.title: Compute once, reuse everywhere
docs.text: The FixtureOutlook dataclass holds one fixture's 1X2 probabilities. Ranking is per entrant, but the score matrix is not, so it is computed once per fixture and shared. The dashboard and the horizon planner both rank the same gameweek repeatedly, and this stops them refitting per entrant.

docs.title: Modelling
docs.text:
• Dixon-Coles with time decay, a tail-tolerance goal grid (min_goals_grid=10, cap 20), rho bounded to ±0.2 and λ clamped to 0.05-6.0
  • Elo, market, Golden Goal and shot-proxy modules sit beside the core. The shot proxy was built, ablated (ablation_009) and rejected
  • engine_status.md uses strict status levels (BUILT, TESTED OFFLINE, LIVE VERIFIED, ACTIVE, SHADOW), so an adapter that exists is never described as live

docs.title: Service layer
docs.text:
• bym serve uses stdlib http.server, with api/contracts.py as the frozen read-model boundary
  • bym tick is stateless and cron-shaped. The web and worker containers share one --db, so jobs the browser schedules are the ones the worker polls
  • Config, rounds, results, data and secrets are bind-mounted from the host, so they stay visible and backupable

docs.title: Evidence trail
docs.text:
• Ablation and baseline results are committed under results/, with the paired-analysis scripts under scripts/
  • A prospective, append-only ledger pre-registers arms. claim_outcomes.py pairs recorded claims with realised results

docs.title: 📊 Key Metrics
docs.text:
• Python tests: 1,176 passed, 6 skipped across 95 test files (full run, 183 seconds)
  • UI tests: 61 passing under node --test
  • Source: 122 Python modules, 32,811 lines under src/
  • CLI: 18 subcommands, including fetch, predict, backtest, tick and lms-pick
  • Specs: SPEC.md 1,313 lines; SPEC_FPL.md 1,636 lines
  • Result records: 14 markdown files in results/

docs.title: 🛠️ Development Process
docs.text:
• Spec-driven - docs/SPEC.md is the source of truth, and section markers such as §22 appear throughout the code
  • Validation protocol - Each season has an assigned role, and modelling choices may not react to holdout results
  • Declared deferrals - xG was closed after four free sources were probed, and the 100 Club annotation is marked not started

This project demonstrates statistical modelling, experimental discipline, and enforcing governance rules in code.

docs.title: No One Saw Everything — Fair-Play Murder Mystery
docs.text:
TL;DR: A Smallville-style murder mystery in which the player arrives after the crime, rewinds the morning, interrogates villagers, and builds a case on a board. The truth is generated and locked before play, and the API never leaks it. LLMs add procedural cases and narrative flavour but never decide what is true.

Stack: Python • FastAPI • Pydantic • React 18 • TypeScript • Vite • pytest • Vitest • Playwright • optional OpenAI-compatible LLM (deterministic fallback by default)

docs.title: ✨ Features
docs.text:
• ⏪ Rewind viewer - Scrub time ranges, filter by location or sim, and pin events to discover clues
  • 🔍 Evidence inspection - Location searches with prerequisite-gated finds
  • 🗂️ Notes and case board - Manual, contradiction and theory notes, pin-to-suspect, a claims ledger and player-owned suspicion levels
  • 🎤 Interview engine - Six question types with answers grounded in seeded memories and lie state
  • 💬 Free-text interrogation - Typed questions are classified, references are resolved, and the question is routed to the same grounded answers (or casual chat)
  • ⚔️ Challenge engine - Confront a claim with discovered evidence, including one villager's testimony against another's, and get scripted outcomes with pressure tracking
  • ⚖️ Accusation judge - Grades killer, motive, method and opportunity; the truth reveal comes only after an accusation
  • 🧬 Procedural generation - LLM-assisted cases from three templates (blackmail, betrayal, debt), with timelines recompiled per case
  • 🛡️ Fairness validator - validate_case() gates every case, hand-authored or generated
  • 🗺️ Playtest tooling - Session telemetry, hints, playtest export and a dev map editor

docs.title: 🧠 Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    Player["Player"] --> UI["React + Vite UI :5173"]
    UI -->|"/api proxy"| API["FastAPI :8010 - main.py"]
    API --> Proj["projections.py - truth firewall"]
    Proj --> Case[("Locked case bundle<br/>solution, memories, clue graph")]
    API --> Session["session.py - mutable player state"]
    API --> Engines["Deterministic engines<br/>interview, challenge, testimony, judge"]
    Engines --> Case
    Engines --> Session
    Engines -.->|"flavour text only"| Rewrite["LLM rewrite"]
    Rewrite --> San["Sanitiser"]
    San -->|"reject: use authored text"| Engines
    Gen["Case generator + timeline compiler"] --> Val["validator.py"]
    Val -->|"zero errors"| Case
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Player
    participant E as challenge.py
    participant S as Session
    participant L as LLM rewrite
    P->>E: Confront claim with clue ids
    E->>S: Were these clues discovered?
    S-->>E: yes or no
    alt undiscovered, mismatched claim, or victim
        E-->>P: Rejected
    else valid
        E->>E: Pick best-matching rule
        E->>S: Update pressure and claim status
        E->>L: Rewrite authored line
        L-->>E: Text or sanitiser rejection
        E-->>P: Outcome with safe text
    end

docs.title: Truth first, flavour second
docs.text: The case is a locked Pydantic model, and the engines compute every outcome deterministically before an LLM sees anything. The LLM is then asked only to rewrite surface dialogue, and a sanitiser rejects rewrites that leak role labels, hidden facts outside a precomputed allow-list, or JSON artefacts, falling back to the authored text. The default fake provider needs no network, so the full test suite runs offline.

docs.title: Fair-play by construction
docs.text: projections.py strips hidden fields at the API boundary, and the reveal is only served after an accusation. Fairness is checked rather than hoped for. validate_case() must pass with zero errors, and it exists because cases once shipped invalid. Its checks include a ban on routine summaries that leak the plot, and the suite has dedicated no-leak tests for projections, LLM dialogue, free-text interviews, generated-case endpoints and open-ended questions.

docs.title: Testimony as evidence
docs.text: The title promises that nobody saw everything, so one villager's word can be used against another's. testimony.py settles whether two statements can both be true. The same person in two places within 5 minutes is a bilocation, and an opposite-polarity claim about the same place within 20 minutes is a denial. The tolerances are deliberately conservative, because a detector that cries wolf teaches players to ignore it.

docs.title: Generated cases that are not reskins
docs.text: A template-only generator replays the same morning every time. In llm_assisted mode a timeline phase writes new ambient beats, and timeline_compiler keeps the murder and every clue-bearing event untouched. It reserves agent-minute slots so nobody is ever in two places, and on any failure it keeps the template. The invariants live in the compiler, not in the LLM prompt.

docs.title: Backend
docs.text:
• Three-way split: immutable case bundle (case_store.py), mutable per-session state (session.py), and player-safe views (projections.py)
  • challenge._find_rule ranks by fully-supplied trigger, then outcome severity, then evidence overlap, so more evidence never yields a weaker response
  • LLM config precedence: saved settings override env vars; providers are fake, auto and openai_compatible, with SSRF guarding in http_safety.py
  • Interview rules that silently never match are caught by a reachability test

docs.title: Frontend
docs.text:
• Views for Rewind, Suspects, Places, Board, Accuse and a case library, plus an accusation ceremony and reveal breakdown
  • Layered location scenes, a map replay, composure meters, and audio via Howler
  • Vitest unit tests plus a Playwright golden-path e2e spec

docs.title: Quality
docs.text:
• pytest doubles as the case-fairness validator, including a golden solve path that plays a case end to end
  • Verdict bands account for correctness, so naming the right killer never reads as "wrong suspect"

docs.title: 📊 Key Metrics
docs.text:
• Backend tests: 748 passed (full run in about 40 seconds) across 70 test files
  • Frontend: 70 TypeScript files, about 22,100 lines; 4 Vitest files and 1 Playwright spec
  • Backend: about 12,900 lines in app/*.py plus about 3,600 in app/llm/; 57 API routes in main.py
  • Cases: 8 authored case bundles (16 to 18 agents and 17 to 25 clues each) plus 1 generated; 3 generation templates
  • Spec docs: 21 markdown design and production docs in docs/
  • Dependencies: 5 lines in requirements.txt; 7 runtime npm packages

docs.title: 🛠️ Development Process
docs.text:
Built phase by phase from a spec pack, from the locked data model through rewind, interview, challenge, judge, generation and free-text interrogation. Later work was driven by playtests (screenshots and QA notes are kept in playtest-evidence/), blind reviewer reports per case, and a production audit. Each bug that shipped in content became a validator check or a regression test, which is why the rules above exist.

This project demonstrates designing LLM-assisted systems around a deterministic source of truth, with fairness enforced by validators and tests rather than by prompts.

docs.title: Voice Harness — Voice AI Evaluation & Assurance
docs.text:
TL;DR: A container-first, deterministic core for evaluating voice AI in banking. It provides synthetic banking fixtures, a mock provider, a hash-chained evidence ledger and Ed25519-signed export bundles, so every test run produces tamper-evident proof. Live provider adapters sit on top for bake-offs, but the core and CI need no credentials.

Stack: Python 3.13 • FastAPI (HTTP + WebSocket) • PostgreSQL 17 (SQLite fallback) • Docker Compose • OpenTelemetry • Ed25519 signing • MCP • Node browser tests

docs.title: ✨ Features
docs.text:
• 🧾 Evidence ledger - Append-only and hash-chained, with export manifests (event count, final ledger hash, per-artifact SHA-256) that are Ed25519-signed over RFC 8785 canonical bytes
  • ✅ Bundle verification - verify-bundle re-checks event count, final ledger hash and artifact hashes offline against a trusted key ring
  • 🛡️ Policy-gated tools - Protected tool proposals are denied before execution, and approval tokens are single-use and consumed transactionally
  • 🔊 PCM playback gate - Audio playback is bound to session, hash, range and epoch
  • 🎙️ Provider bake-offs - Compare 2 to 6 live configurations (OpenAI, Nova Sonic, xAI, Gemini, ElevenLabs) on the same scenarios, with Wilson-interval scorecards and McNemar head-to-heads computed from the ledgers
  • 🎭 Scenario catalogue - 3 mock built-ins plus 40 live scenarios in five groups: happy path, identity, vulnerable customers, faults and payments
  • 🔌 MCP surface - stdio MCP server and a correlated tool-call gateway
  • 📏 Benchmarks and perf gate - Component benchmarks checked against a committed baseline in CI, plus opt-in load and PostgreSQL-outage chaos tests
  • 🔑 Key lifecycle - Signing keys can be rotated (old public keys stay in a hash-chained history) or revoked, which makes every signature by that key fail

docs.title: 🧠 Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    Op["Operator / CI"] --> API["Authenticated FastAPI"]
    API --> Engine["engine.py<br/>trusted orchestration + synthetic banking tools"]
    Engine --> Policy["policy / approvals / verdicts"]
    Engine --> Ledger[("Evidence ledger<br/>PostgreSQL")]
    Engine --> Prov["Mock + live providers"]
    Ledger --> Bundle["Signed export bundle"]
    Bundle --> Verify["verify-bundle"]
    API --> Web["Browser playback client"]
    Engine --> OTel["OTLP collector"]
flowchart LR
    Bench["make benchmark"] --> Run["perf-run.json"]
    Run --> Check["perf_gate check"]
    Base["artifacts/perf-baseline.json"] --> Check
    Check -->|"p95 within limit"| Pass["CI passes"]
    Check -->|"fails"| Retry["rerun once from a fresh benchmark"]
    Retry -->|"fails again"| Fail["CI fails"]
    Retry -->|"passes"| Pass

docs.title: Invariants that fail closed
docs.text: A failure to write evidence blocks tool calls and releases, while a failure to export a trace must not lose ledger data. The asymmetry is deliberate: the ledger is the source of truth, telemetry is a convenience. Contracts (JSON Schema and OpenAPI under contracts/) are generated from the pydantic models, and test_contracts_in_sync.py fails on any drift because the generator is deterministic.

docs.title: Signing that names its own key
docs.text: The bundle carries a detached envelope of {algorithm, key_id, payload_sha256, value}, and the manifest names the same key id and algorithm, so the key choice is itself signed. Verification is offline and only trusts public keys the verifier supplies. If no signer is configured a manifest declares unsigned_local rather than pretending otherwise.

docs.title: A perf gate tuned for noisy runners
docs.text: perf_gate.py fails a run on any timeout, failure, dropped or discontinuous sample, a short sample (under 1000 observations), a missing profile, or a p95 above max(baseline x 2.0, baseline + 5 ms). The tolerance is wide on purpose: it exists to catch order-of-magnitude regressions such as connection-per-event, not 10% drift. The baseline merges 4 runs and keeps the worst p50/p95 per profile, and a failing CI gate reruns once so a one-off runner stall does not block a merge.

docs.title: Honest measurement
docs.text: Benchmarks are explicitly component measurements, not end-to-end latency. Fixture audio is PCM silence with scripted metadata, so the tests prove enforcement mechanics, not ASR or audibility. The docs say so.

docs.title: Evidence & Storage
docs.text:
• Transactional per-run namespaces over a psycopg pool, with a SQLite fallback for local development
  • chaos_postgres stops and restarts the database mid-run with client-style retries, and exits 0 only if no evidence was lost, duplicated or unverifiable

docs.title: Policy & Contracts
docs.text:
• Pydantic schemas reject unexpected properties; approval-token signing lives in approvals.py
  • 135 generated contract files cover events, tools and approval tokens

docs.title: Supply Chain
docs.text:
• Dependencies are pinned in pyproject.toml and hash-locked in requirements.lock
  • The Python, Node, PostgreSQL and OTel collector images are all pinned by digest
  • Tests run in a non-root container against real PostgreSQL

docs.title: Testing & CI
docs.text: • unittest suite plus Node browser tests; the GitHub Actions workflow runs make test then make perf-gate

  • Tests: 90 Python test files with 1,212 test methods, plus 18 Node browser test files with 195 test/it cases
  • Acceptance gates: AC-01 to AC-21, mapped in docs/PHASE1_STATUS.md
  • Scenarios: 40 live catalogue scenarios, plus 3 mock built-ins
  • Bake-off scale: up to 6 providers x 40 scenarios x 3 repetitions, which is 720 cells; the full set has been run

docs.title: Connect SRE Agent — AI Operations for Amazon Connect
docs.text:
TL;DR: A domain-specific SRE platform for Amazon Connect. It detects contact-flow regressions, correlates infrastructure changes with incidents, calculates blast radius and recommends safe remediation. A supervisor agent coordinates 10 read-only specialists. Writes to Connect are off by default, and every change passes an operator approval and a policy gate before it runs.

Stack: Python • FastAPI • Google ADK (Gemini) • AWS Strands (Bedrock Claude) • Lambda • EventBridge • DynamoDB • SQS • CloudFormation • ECS Fargate • React 19 + Vite • Docker

docs.title: ✨ Features
docs.text:
• 🧠 10 specialist agents - FLOW, MODULE, QUEUE, LEXA, AIA, CHANGE, IMPACT, RUNBOOK, RISK and VERIFY, each scoped to a subset of tools
  • 🔀 Two model paths - Gemini via ADK or Claude on Bedrock via Strands, switched with the MODEL_PROVIDER variable
  • 🗺️ Topology graph - A scanner Lambda crawls Connect APIs into a DynamoDB adjacency list, so blast radius is a graph traversal
  • ✋ Human approval - Only the supervisor can call propose_remediation; the operator approves in the UI before the dispatcher Lambda will act
  • 📡 Event ingestion - CloudWatch alarms, Connect flow logs and CloudTrail mutations are normalised, de-duplicated and turned into incidents
  • 🧾 Investigation memory - recall_prior_incidents and record_investigation_memory let agents reuse earlier findings
  • 📚 Seeded policies and runbooks - Policies, tool registry, journeys and 7 runbooks are loaded by seed scripts
  • 🎛️ 14-page operator UI - Incidents, approvals, topology, monitoring, agent swarm, Connect AI agents, policy and runbooks
  • 🔁 Demo and live modes - A header toggle switches most endpoints between mock data and real AWS and Connect APIs

docs.title: 🧠 Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    EB["EventBridge<br/>alarms, flow logs, CloudTrail"] --> Norm[normalizer Lambda]
    Norm --> DDB[("DynamoDB incidents")]
    Norm -->|"POST /api/incidents"| API[FastAPI runtime]
    API -->|background task| Sup[Supervisor agent]
    Sup --> Spec["10 read-only specialists"]
    Spec --> Tools["Topology, CloudWatch, Connect and runbook tools"]
    Sup -->|propose_remediation| Appr[("Approval record")]
    Appr --> UI[Operator UI]
    UI -->|approve| Disp["action_dispatcher Lambda<br/>gates A to D"]
    Disp --> Connect[Amazon Connect]
sequenceDiagram
    participant S as Supervisor
    participant T as propose_remediation
    participant P as Policy table
    participant O as Operator
    participant D as action_dispatcher
    S->>T: action, params, justification
    T->>P: scan enabled policies
    T->>T: compute blast radius, depth 3
    alt policy violated
        T-->>S: BLOCKED with reason
    else allowed
        T->>O: approval record, PENDING
        O->>D: approve
        D->>D: gates A to D
        D-->>O: executed or denied
    end

docs.title: Policy enforced twice, in code
docs.text: Safety does not live in the prompt. propose_remediation reads the enabled policies from DynamoDB and can return BLOCKED before any ticket exists: out-of-hours deployments (22:00-06:00 UTC), and a max blast radius of 20% of topology nodes. The dispatcher Lambda then applies four independent gates: Connect writes enabled (A), high-risk actions need an approval ticket (B), autonomous operation needs its own flag (C), and the ticket must be marked APPROVED (D). A confused model cannot skip either layer.

docs.title: One toolset, two agent frameworks
docs.text: Tools in runtime/tools.py are plain typed Python functions with docstrings, so the same implementations run under Google ADK and AWS Strands without modification. agent.py picks the provider at import time. On Strands, agents_bedrock.py builds each specialist as an Agent wrapped in @tool, and gives only the supervisor propose_remediation, so specialists stay read-only by construction. Adding a specialist takes a prompt, an agent wrapper and a supervisor persona entry.

docs.title: Blast radius as a graph query
docs.text: The topology scanner stores nodes and edges as an adjacency list: nodeId plus edgeTypeTarget, with DEPENDS_ON# and REQUIRED_BY# edge prefixes. Blast radius is a depth-limited upstream traversal, and the result is attached to the approval record so the operator sees impacted nodes next to the proposed action.

docs.title: Realistic operational constraints
docs.text: The repo includes scripted Lambda deploys, synthetic alarm tests and a dev-IP security group updater. It also documents the real constraints: the topology scanner must run before blast radius is meaningful, and alarms must carry Connect resource dimensions to be correlated.

docs.title: Agent runtime
docs.text:
• _BedrockSupervisor.chat() runs the synchronous Strands agent in a thread-pool executor so FastAPI's event loop is never blocked
  • Investigations run as FastAPI background tasks, so the normalizer's POST returns immediately
  • _compress_tool_output passes tool payloads through headroom before the agent sees them, falling back to the raw payload on any error
  • Defaults: gemini-3.5-flash for ADK, us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6 for Bedrock

docs.title: Event pipeline and data
docs.text:
• normalizer.py de-duplicates within DEDUPE_WINDOW_MINUTES and triggers a topology refresh on CloudTrail mutations
  • 11 DynamoDB tables cover incidents, approvals, policy, topology, agent runs, agent steps, journeys, tool registry and memory; agent steps expire after 90 days
  • Approvals move through PENDING, AUTO_APPROVED, approved or rejected; a SEV4 policy can auto-approve low-severity changes

docs.title: Infrastructure
docs.text:
• One CloudFormation template defines the VPC, ALB, ECS Fargate service, Lambda roles, DynamoDB tables, EventBridge rules and SQS queues
  • Feature flags EnableConnectWriteActions and EnableAutonomousActions both default to false
  • A flow-log subscription filter is only created when PrimaryConnectInstanceId is supplied

docs.title: 📊 Key Metrics
docs.text:
• Agents: 1 supervisor plus 10 specialists, 17 tool functions in tools.py
  • API: 38 route handlers in runtime/main.py (1,988 lines)
  • Code: about 4,100 lines of runtime Python, 1,700 lines of Lambda and seed Python, 4,550 lines of UI JSX across 28 files
  • Infrastructure: 1,452-line CloudFormation template with 11 DynamoDB tables, 3 Lambda functions, 6 EventBridge rules, 2 SQS queues
  • Operations: 13 deploy, seed and test scripts; 9 seeded policies; 7 runbooks
  • Docs: 1,800-line SPEC.md plus 6 documents in docs/
  • Tests: test_agent.py has 4 checks (tool signatures, Strands registry, supervisor build, live Bedrock call)

docs.title: 🛠️ Development Process
docs.text:
The project is spec-driven: SPEC.md and the architecture, policy-model, topology and runbook-authoring documents in docs/ define the design, and the repo carries a CLAUDE.md for Claude Code. Each Lambda has its own deploy script and a synthetic test script, so infrastructure changes can be exercised without waiting for a real incident.

This project demonstrates multi-agent orchestration, event-driven AWS architecture and layered safe-autonomy patterns for operations.

docs.title: Connect AI Agent Demo Builder
docs.text:
TL;DR: A local Next.js tool for configuring, previewing, deploying and live-testing an Amazon Q in Connect AI agent demo. It manages two agents (CustomerIntentRouter and LostCard), builds the AWS SDK payloads, and uses Bedrock to generate Contact Flow JSON from a journey config. A banking lost-card scenario with simulated tool failures drives the demo.

Stack: Next.js 16 • React 19 • TypeScript • Tailwind CSS 4 • Zustand • Zod • AWS SDK (qconnect, connect, connectparticipant, bedrock-runtime, sts) • amazon-connect-streams • Amazon Chime SDK • React Flow (@xyflow/react)

docs.title: ✨ Features
docs.text:
• ⚙️ Settings and agents - Configure region, assistant ID, Connect instance and deployment mode, and edit both agent prompts with YAML validation and reset-to-default
  • 👀 Preview and dry run - Inspect the generated prompt and agent payloads before anything touches AWS
  • 🚀 Staged deploy - Four modes: preview_only, create_prompts_only, create_agents_only, create_prompts_and_agents, with duplicate detection and step-by-step progress
  • 🎭 Failure simulation - Nine demo modes, such as lookup_stage_failure, tool_failure_at_block_card and full_success_simulation, plus eight mock banking tools
  • 🔎 Flow discovery - Fetch real Connect flows and parse their block schemas into a reusable library
  • 🧩 Experience builder - Configure a journey and routing rules, generate Contact Flow JSON via Bedrock, then deploy it
  • ✅ Flow verification - A second Bedrock call explains the generated flow in plain English and lists issues and suggestions
  • 🗺️ Flow canvas - Read-only React Flow graph of the generated Contact Flow
  • 📞 Live testing - Test through WebRTC voice or Connect chat directly in the tool
  • 📐 Documented architecture - C4 levels 1 to 3 plus key data flows in docs/architecture.md

docs.title: 🧠 Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    User["Demo builder"] --> Pages["App Router pages<br/>9 routes"]
    Pages --> Stores[("Zustand + localStorage<br/>project, experience, schema stores")]
    Pages --> Test["WebRTCTester / ConnectChatTester<br/>amazon-connect-streams"]
    Pages -->|fetch| API["26 API route handlers"]
    API --> Lib["src/lib<br/>payloads, flow, prompts, aws clients"]
    Lib --> QC["Amazon Q in Connect<br/>prompts and agents"]
    Lib --> Conn["Amazon Connect<br/>flows, queues, contacts"]
    Lib --> BR["Amazon Bedrock<br/>flow generate and verify"]
    Test --> Conn

The experience flow is a generate, verify, deploy loop:

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as Builder
    participant S as Schema store
    participant G as flowGenerator
    participant B as Bedrock
    participant C as Connect
    U->>C: Discover existing flows
    C-->>S: Parsed block schemas
    U->>G: Journey config + agent context
    G->>B: System prompt with schemas
    B-->>G: Flow JSON
    Note over G: Strip fences, JSON.parse, retry once on failure
    G-->>U: Flow JSON + logs
    U->>G: Verify
    G->>B: Explain and review flow
    B-->>U: Explanation, issues, suggestions
    U->>C: Deploy flow and test

docs.title: Schemas learned from real flows
docs.text: Connect's Contact Flow block format is large and under-documented, so the tool does not hard-code it. schemaParser.ts parses flows fetched from the user's own instance, extracts block schemas into a library, and flowGenerator.ts serialises that library into the Bedrock system prompt. The model is constrained to block shapes that exist in the target instance.

docs.title: Agent context in the prompt
docs.text: The generator also receives the entry agent's name, description, system prompt and tool list. Compare-block conditions can then use the exact tool names the agent signals through session attributes, instead of invented values.

docs.title: Defensive handling of model output
docs.text: Generated JSON is stripped of markdown fences and parsed. On failure it is retried once with the parse error fed back, and every step is logged. Verification returns an explicit error when the model's reply is not valid JSON, so unreliable output is flagged rather than shown as fact.

docs.title: No server-side state
docs.text: Configuration lives in persisted Zustand stores in the browser. AWS credentials come from the host's default credential chain and stay in the API routes, so the browser never holds them.

docs.title: Frontend
docs.text:
• Four Zustand stores: projectStore, experienceStore and schemaStore persisted to localStorage, and an ephemeral logStore
  • Zod schemas (src/lib/config/schema.ts) validate project config, deployment modes and name-suffix modes
  • WebRTCTester reaches window.connect.RTCSession from amazon-connect-streams at call time and shows a clear error if the global is missing, because amazon-connect-rtc-js does not exist on npm (recorded in BUILD_LOG.md)

docs.title: API layer
docs.text:
• 26 route handlers wrap Q in Connect, Connect and Bedrock, including chat start, message and transcript, DTMF, queues, phone numbers, Lex bots and a streaming Bedrock chat
  • deployService.ts paginates existing prompts and agents to detect duplicates, and resolves the account ID through STS when an agent ARN must be built
  • validatePromptYaml checks for a top-level messages array before deploy

docs.title: Docs and IAM
docs.text:
• IAM_PERMISSIONS.md and iam-policy.json document the permissions the tool needs
  • Separate prerequisites and troubleshooting guides sit alongside the C4 architecture doc

docs.title: 📊 Key Metrics
docs.text:
• Source: 74 TypeScript files, 9,345 lines under src/
  • Routes: 9 pages and 26 API route handlers
  • Agents: 2 managed Q in Connect agents and 8 mock tools
  • Simulation: 9 demo failure and success modes, 4 deployment modes
  • Dependencies: 16 runtime and 10 dev packages
  • Docs: 4 docs files (567 lines), IAM guide and policy
  • Tests: No automated test suite; verification is via npm run build and lint

docs.text:
Built in phases recorded in BUILD_LOG.md: packages, foundation, flow discovery, experience builder, WebRTC tester, then navigation and dashboard. The log notes each phase's build status and the blockers hit along the way. The final entry records a passing npm run build. It also records 63 lint errors and 5 warnings that pre-date the experience work. AGENTS.md warns the coding agent that this Next.js version has breaking changes and to read the bundled docs first.

docs.title: AI Darts — Three-Camera Computer Vision Scoring
docs.text:
TL;DR: A darts scoring system that uses three USB cameras and classical computer vision to find where each dart lands. A dart is only scored when several cameras agree on its tip, and a game engine with X01 plus ten other modes sits on top, driving a broadcast-style React UI.

Stack: Python • OpenCV • NumPy • FastAPI • WebSocket • React 19 • Vite • Tailwind CSS v4 • Kokoro TTS

docs.title: ✨ Features
docs.text:
• 📷 Multi-camera detection - Background subtraction per camera, with each view mapped into a single 500×500 canonical board space by homography
  • 🎯 Line-based tip localisation - Each dart shaft is fitted as a line, warped into board space, and the intersection across cameras gives the true tip
  • 🧭 Alignment and auto-calibration - Drag four diamond handles to fit the board mesh, or auto-fit the board outline as an ellipse and just rotate to line up the numbers
  • 🎮 Game engine - X01 (301/501/701, straight/double/master check-in, double-out, legs and sets) with a checkout solver, plus ten more modes including Cricket, Killer, Shanghai and Around the Clock
  • 🤖 AI opponents - Three skill levels (Gaussian spread of 45, 15 and 6 mm) that pick mode-appropriate targets
  • ↩️ Correction controls - Undo, click-the-board to correct a misread dart, review mode, and background recapture
  • 🎬 Cinematic mode - Walk-on cards, themed rules cards, per-mode scoreboards, confetti, and an MC voice synthesised in the browser
  • 📊 Stats and tournaments - Match history, leaderboard, head-to-head endpoint and a tournament bracket
  • 🔌 Pluggable detection - An adapter lets the Autodarts board manager replace the native vision engine, with a mock server for development without hardware

docs.title: 🧠 Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    C0[Camera 0] --> Det
    C1[Camera 1] --> Det
    C2[Camera 2] --> Det
    Align["alignment.json<br/>per-camera homographies"] --> Det["detect.py<br/>background diff and contours"]
    Det --> Tips["line_tips.py<br/>shaft lines to canonical tip"]
    Tips --> Track["Multi-target tracker<br/>settle, contamination and agreement gates"]
    Track --> Game["game.py and games.py<br/>X01 plus 10 modes"]
    Auto["autodarts_adapter.py<br/>optional engine"] -.-> Game
    Game --> API["FastAPI server.py<br/>REST and /ws/game"]
    API --> UI["React UI<br/>Live Track, Align, Stats, Cinematic"]

The tracker is the part worth a second diagram. A dart moves through these states before it is allowed to score:

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Watching: empty board
    Watching --> Pending: new cluster seen by 2+ cameras
    Pending --> Pending: persists, consecutive multi-camera frames
    Pending --> Forgotten: unseen for grace frames
    Pending --> Scored: persisted, full agreement, scene settled and clean
    Scored --> Watching: visit continues
    Scored --> AllDone: visit over
    AllDone --> Watching: board cleared
    Forgotten --> Watching

docs.title: Fighting phantoms, not finding darts
docs.text: Finding a dart is the easy half. Most of the engineering goes into refusing to score things that are not darts: flight ends, a throwing arm, lighting drift. Every candidate sits in a pending state and must pass several independent gates before it counts. The scene has to be settled (frame-to-frame foreground change below a threshold), no camera may show more than a maximum number of blobs (an arm shatters into many contours), and the dart must have reached full camera agreement and still have multi-camera support on the confirming frame. When several candidates are ready at once, the tightest spread wins, then camera count, then persistence, so a long-lived edge artifact cannot outrank a fresh real dart.

docs.title: Geometry that exploits the flights
docs.text: Dart flights sit about 10 cm above the board plane, so a homography maps a flight end to a different canonical point in each camera, while the tip, on the plane, lands consistently. The original approach projected both shaft endpoints and clustered them. The current one fits a shaft line per camera and intersects the warped lines, which removes endpoint ambiguity entirely. Cluster tightness is camera-count dependent, because a loose two-camera match is the signature of a phantom.

docs.title: Not absorbing darts into the background
docs.text: An earlier idea was to fold scored darts into the reference image. It created blind spots around them, so a nearby dart was seen by too few cameras and missed. The design now diffs against the empty board only and leaves phantom rejection to the gates. Board-clear is judged relative to the darts-in foreground level, so an arm spiking the signal while pulling darts is not mistaken for a cleared board.

docs.title: One interface for every game mode
docs.text: All eleven games share the X01-compatible interface (record_hit, undo, to_dict, review), created through a create_game factory. to_dict() carries a per-mode state block, so one scoreboard and cinematic UI render any mode.

docs.title: Vision pipeline
docs.text:
• Detection runs in a background thread and publishes the latest annotated JPEG, so closing the Live Track tab detaches a viewer without losing the background or missing darts
  • Tracker thresholds are named constants at the top of detect.py, with notes on which direction to move each one
  • Warm-up drains frames and averages 30 unique frames for the background; the board mask comes deterministically from the alignment homography
  • While the board is empty the background is blended (alpha 0.05) to heal lighting drift

docs.title: Backend
docs.text:
• FastAPI streams MJPEG and receives mouse and keyboard events back through event lists the detection worker drains
  • A lifespan-managed watcher diffs game state every 100 ms and broadcasts over /ws/game, catching both detection-thread scoring and REST mutations
  • Per-session logs tee stdout and stderr, with old sessions pruned

docs.title: Frontend
docs.text:
• Kokoro TTS runs in-browser via WASM with a managed speech queue, SSML parsing, and a two-tier cache (in-memory LRU and IndexedDB)
  • Speech lines have a TTL, so stale commentary is dropped rather than read out late

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
• A replay harness feeds recorded camera sessions through the same step_tracker function the live loop calls, so scoring bugs reproduce without cameras
  • Unit tests cover the game engines, checkout solver, calibration, consensus clustering, line tips and the Autodarts adapter

docs.title: 📊 Key Metrics
docs.text:
• Python source: 8,289 lines across 23 modules in src/
  • Frontend: 24 JS/JSX files, 9,116 lines
  • Tests: 8 test files, 1,347 lines
  • Game modes: 11 (X01 plus 10 in games.py)
  • API surface: 28 REST and WebSocket routes in server.py
  • Cameras: 3 USB cameras into one 500×500 canonical space

docs.title: 🛠️ Development Process
docs.text:
Built iteratively against a real rig. Each misscore was diagnosed from recorded sessions and turned into a gate, a tuned constant or a replay test. Several approaches were tried and replaced, and the reasons are kept in the project notes so they are not retried.

This project demonstrates applied computer vision, multi-view geometry and robustness engineering for a real-world, noisy physical setup.

docs.title: Local LLM Gateway — Routing Across a Home AI Cluster
docs.text:
TL;DR: A lightweight OpenAI-compatible gateway that routes chat requests across a local LLM cluster: Ollama on a Windows/CUDA PC and LM Studio-style servers on a MacBook. Routing, privacy tiers and model aliases live in YAML. It ships a live dashboard and a mobile-first chat UI whose history and memory stay in the browser.

Stack: Python • FastAPI • Pydantic • Ollama • LM Studio • YAML policy config • aiosqlite + JSONL telemetry • IndexedDB • SearXNG • trafilatura

docs.title: ✨ Features
docs.text:
• 🔌 Drop-in API - /v1/chat/completions, /v1/models and /v1/embeddings work with any OpenAI-compatible client
  • 🧭 Policy-based routing - Five named routes (local-fast, local-quality, private-docs, local-fast-apple, cloud-best), each with a primary, a fallback and an allowed privacy list
  • 🤖 Rule-based auto-routing - The auto alias scores the prompt for privacy, quality and speed signals and picks a route with no LLM call
  • 🔒 Privacy tiers - A request's tier comes from the x-ai-privacy header, then metadata.privacy, then the configured default. Routes that don't allow the tier are blocked
  • 🌐 Web grounding - The web alias searches a self-hosted SearXNG, fetches the top pages and answers from the extracted text with cited sources
  • 📊 Observability dashboard - Backend health, routing events and stats, plus trace, log and audit-export endpoints
  • 📱 Mobile-first chat UI - Served at /chat/, with conversation history and long-term memory in IndexedDB
  • 📎 Document extraction - /chat/extract pulls text from PDF and DOCX uploads
  • 🔐 Optional HTTPS - Needed for browser microphone access, with a self-signed cert helper
  • 🍓 Headless deployment - A systemd unit and per-node setup scripts, including a Raspberry Pi gateway node

docs.title: 🧠 Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Client["Chat UI / OpenAI clients"] --> GW["FastAPI gateway"]
    GW --> Priv["Privacy check"]
    Priv --> Auto["Auto-route<br/>if model is auto"]
    Auto --> Route["resolve_model_to_route"]
    Priv --> Route
    Route --> Sel["select_backend"]
    Sel --> Ol["Ollama<br/>Windows + CUDA"]
    Sel --> LM["MacBook servers<br/>OpenAI-compatible"]
    GW --> Web["Web grounding<br/>SearXNG"]
    GW --> Tel["Telemetry<br/>metadata only"]
    Tel --> Dash["Dashboard"]
    Cfg["4 YAML files<br/>+ local override"] -.-> Route
    Cfg -.-> Priv
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant G as Gateway
    participant P as Privacy policy
    participant B as Primary backend
    participant F as Fallback backend
    C->>G: POST /v1/chat/completions
    G->>P: tier from header, metadata or default
    P-->>G: allowed or blocked for route
    G->>B: forward request
    alt backend unavailable
        G->>F: retry on fallback
        F-->>G: response
    else healthy
        B-->>G: response
    end
    G-->>C: reply + x-ai-route, x-ai-backend, x-ai-fallback-used

docs.title: Routing as Pure Config
docs.text: Backends, routes, model aliases and security rules are four YAML files, and a gitignored backends.local.yaml overrides the committed one so LAN addresses never reach the repo. Adding a node or changing which machine serves local-quality is an edit, not a deploy. A backend with inference_enabled: false is visible on the dashboard but never selected, which is how the utility node is handled.

docs.title: Forced RAG Instead of Tool-Calling
docs.text: Small local models summarise text they are given far more reliably than they decide to call a tool. So web grounding is a fixed retrieve-then-answer step: search SearXNG, fetch the top results, extract readable text and inject it as a strict system message. Sources come back in an x-ai-sources header and grounding state in x-ai-grounding. Failures degrade to a normal completion rather than an error.

docs.title: Privacy That Also Covers the Search Path
docs.text: SearXNG keeps the query on the LAN, but page fetches leave it. Web grounding is therefore gated separately in security.yaml by privacy tier, and a request at a disallowed tier still gets an answer, just ungrounded. cloud-best is disabled with status: not_configured, and cloud fallback is refused for restricted requests regardless of route config.

docs.title: A Stateless Gateway With a Stateful Client
docs.text: Conversation history and long-term memory live in the browser's IndexedDB, so the shared LAN endpoint needs no login and holds no user data. The cost is that history doesn't follow you between devices. That is a deliberate trade for a household service used mostly from phones.

docs.title: Routing and Policy
docs.text:
• routing.py (resolve_model_to_route, select_backend) is pure config logic with no I/O, so it is directly unit-testable
  • autoroute.py scores regex signal lists: any privacy hit goes to private-docs, two or more quality hits or a prompt of 400+ characters goes to local-quality, and short or fast-signal prompts go to local-fast
  • A confidential or restricted privacy header overrides content scanning
  • Every response carries x-ai-route, x-ai-backend, x-ai-model, x-ai-fallback-used and x-ai-policy, plus x-ai-auto-reason for auto-routed requests

docs.title: Providers and Telemetry
docs.text:
• An abstract Provider base with Ollama, LM Studio and generic OpenAI-compatible implementations
  • Telemetry records routing metadata to JSONL and two SQLite tables (llm_requests, llm_events), and prompt content is never logged (prompt_logging_enabled: false)

docs.title: Chat Client
docs.text:
• Plain ES modules with no build step: db.js, history.js, memory.js, settings.js and app.js
  • Shell height follows window.visualViewport so the composer stays above the iOS soft keyboard. Form fields are 16px on mobile to stop focus-zoom, and Enter sends only on non-coarse pointers

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
• Per-role node folders (fast-coder, quality, gateway, hub), a SearXNG docker-compose, and gateway.service for systemd
  • manage.sh starts and stops the gateway and turns on HTTPS automatically when certs/server.{crt,key} exist

docs.title: 📊 Key Metrics
docs.text:
• Endpoints: 19 in server.py plus 6 observability routes in api_observability.py
  • Routes / aliases: 5 routes, 10 model aliases, 4 backends (3 inference-enabled, 1 utility node)
  • Code: 2,282 lines of Python in gateway/ and 970 in tests/; about 2,100 lines of chat client HTML and JS
  • Tests: 58 test functions across 10 files; test_live_backends.py skips itself when LAN nodes are unreachable
  • Spec docs: 5 in docs/, covering the fabric, chat memory, observability, Open WebUI and dashboard plan
  • Dependencies: 11 packages in requirements.txt

docs.title: 🛠️ Development Process
docs.text:
The design started from the spec docs in docs/, then grew outward from the routing core to the dashboard, the chat client and the Raspberry Pi deployment. Most tests run offline against the FastAPI app with httpx, so routing and privacy rules can be checked without any GPU node being up. Live-backend checks are separate scripts (check_backends.py, smoke_gateway.py) for when the cluster is running.

This project demonstrates LLM infrastructure: provider abstraction, policy enforcement and privacy-by-design for self-hosted models.

docs.title: WhatsForTea — Kitchen Assistant for the NAS
docs.text:
TL;DR: A self-hosted recipe manager that digitises physical recipe cards with a vision model, then answers one question: what can I actually cook tonight, given what is in my kitchen right now? Pantry stock is tracked as a confidence value that decays over time, recipes are scored against it, and a LangGraph chat assistant (TeaBot) can act on the pantry with human approval. It runs as Docker containers on a Synology NAS.

Stack: Python 3.12 • FastAPI • Next.js 15 • PostgreSQL 16 • Redis 7 • LangGraph • AWS Bedrock (Claude Sonnet and Haiku) • APScheduler • arq • Docker Compose

docs.title: ✨ Features
docs.text:
• 📸 Recipe card scanning - Photos of a card's front and back go to a Claude vision model, which extracts ingredients, steps and per-step crop boxes; a review step flags unresolved ingredients before saving
  • 🔗 More import routes - Recipe URL import, receipt scanning and barcode lookup (Open Food Facts, cached in Redis)
  • 🥫 Confidence-based pantry - Items carry a confidence multiplier, decay daily by category, and can switch to expiry-date-driven confidence
  • 🍳 Hangry matcher - Every recipe gets a 0-100 score from pantry availability, bucketed into Cook Now, Almost There and Planner, plus a "use it up" re-ranking mode
  • 🗓️ Meal planning and shopping - Week planner with auto-fill, shopping list with pack-size rounding rules
  • 🤖 TeaBot - LangGraph chat agent with a Postgres checkpointer, SSE streaming and human-in-the-loop pantry updates
  • 🎙️ Voice commands and nutrition - Haiku-backed intent parsing and nutrition estimates
  • 👨‍👩‍👧 Households - JWT cookie auth, invite codes, per-household data and password reset

docs.title: Confidence instead of counts
docs.text: Nobody weighs their flour. Pantry items store a quantity and a confidence, and the usable amount is quantity × confidence. A daily job lowers confidence (fridge items by 0.1, pantry items by 0.02), and when an expiry date is known, confidence follows days remaining against category shelf life instead. The matcher then scores each ingredient as min(available / required, 1.0) and averages, so "probably have it" counts for partial credit rather than failing a binary check.

docs.title: Model tiering through configuration
docs.text: Vision work (card scanning, auto-crop) routes to Claude Sonnet; routine text work (TeaBot, normaliser, nutrition, voice) routes to Haiku. The split lives in one function, _model_id(vision=...), driven by two environment variables, and prompts are Jinja2 templates in agent_config/ rather than Python strings. Swapping a model or editing a prompt needs no code change.

docs.title: The model proposes, the server writes
docs.text: TeaBot never mutates the pantry directly. A pantry confirmation calls LangGraph's interrupt(), the stream emits hitl_waiting, and only /chat/resume with the user's decision triggers the upsert, executed server-side. The Postgres checkpointer keeps the thread alive across requests, history is trimmed to the last 20 messages, and context is capped at 150 recipes with full ingredient detail for only the top 8 pantry matches.

docs.title: Home-lab pragmatism
docs.text: Scheduling is APScheduler inside the API process, with no Celery; the heavier ingestion and nutrition jobs go to a small arq worker on the existing Redis. Images are built for linux/amd64 with buildx and pulled on the NAS, where a nightly job backs up to a mounted volume.

docs.title: Backend
docs.text:
• Four-layer ingredient normaliser: alias lookup, rapidfuzz fuzzy match (auto-accept at 0.85), LLM assist below 0.60, then user overrides persisted as aliases
  • Uniform error envelope with SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE codes defined in one errors.py
  • Raw LLM responses stored in a separate llm_outputs table with a nightly cleanup job
  • Reservations table prevents the planner and an active cooking session double-counting the same stock

docs.title: Frontend
docs.text:
• Next.js App Router with React Query; next.config.ts rewrites /api/* so the browser only talks to one container
  • TeaBot panel handles the SSE stream and renders human-in-the-loop confirmation widgets
  • Barcode scanning via the BarcodeDetector API with a manual-entry fallback

docs.title: Infrastructure and testing
docs.text:
• Dev compose runs db, redis, api, worker, frontend and aimock; the Synology compose pulls prebuilt images for db, redis, api, worker and frontend
  • AIMock replays recorded Bedrock responses, so tests run without AWS credentials; make record-fixtures refreshes them
  • CI runs Gitleaks secret scanning plus backend tests against real Postgres and Redis service containers

docs.title: Physio — Exercise Illustrations with a Generation Pipeline
docs.text:
TL;DR: A Next.js 16 physio app backed by an internal Asset Lab. Exercise instructions are extracted from web pages with Gemini, then a queue-driven pipeline generates consistent illustrations locally with SDXL via ComfyUI. Each image is checked by Gemini vision and only becomes an app asset after human sign-off.

Stack: Next.js 16 • React 19 • TypeScript • Tailwind 4 • Framer Motion • ComfyUI • SDXL (IP-Adapter + ControlNet) • Gemini 2.5 Flash • JSON file persistence

docs.title: ✨ Features
docs.text:
• 🌐 Exercise extraction - /api/extract scrapes a page with cheerio and asks Gemini to turn it into structured exercises and steps, stored in exerciseLibrary.json
  • 🧍 Locked personas - Two persona definitions (fitness_female_v1, fitness_male_v1) and shared style and negative-prompt constants keep every illustration on-model
  • 🖼️ Master references - The first approved asset for a persona becomes the IP-Adapter reference for all later generations
  • 🦴 Pose control - Registered OpenPose skeletons condition each frame, and an in-browser canvas editor lets you drag 18 joints to author new ones
  • 🧪 Workflow tiers - Reference plus pose, reference only, or text only, chosen by probing ComfyUI's /object_info for the required custom nodes
  • 🔍 Vision QA - Gemini 2.5 Flash returns pass, pass_with_warnings or reject against a hard-failure rubric (wrong pose, cropped body, extra limbs, photorealism, watermark)
  • ✅ Human approval - Vision-passed images stay auto_candidate until approved in the Asset Lab, which moves the file from generated/ to approved/
  • 🔁 Job queue - File-backed jobs with deduplication, three attempts per job, and a worker that pauses when ComfyUI is unreachable
  • 🧰 Safe dev mode - A mock image provider is the default, so the app runs without a GPU or API key

Job and asset state machine:

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> queued
    queued --> generating_image
    generating_image --> vision_validating: PNG saved
    generating_image --> retrying: provider error
    vision_validating --> auto_candidate: pass
    vision_validating --> retrying: reject
    retrying --> generating_image: attempts remain
    retrying --> vision_rejected: attempts exhausted
    auto_candidate --> approved: human approves
    auto_candidate --> human_rejected: human rejects

docs.title: Diagnose by Model Family, Not by Prompt
docs.text: Output quality depends on which model family actually resolved. LocalComfyProvider.getModelConfig() checks, in order, a FORCE_SD15 override, the IMAGE_MODEL_FAMILY env var, a per-request override, then defaults to SDXL (or Flux for .gguf checkpoints). One stale environment variable can silently force an older model, so the project's rule is to check the logged family before touching prompts.

docs.title: Identity Through Constraints
docs.text: Consistency does not rely on one clever prompt. Persona text, illustration style and negative prompts live in assetPrompts.ts, a reference image anchors the face and outfit via IP-Adapter, and a pose skeleton fixes the body. Each of the three layers narrows what the model can vary.

docs.title: Layered Gates With a Human Last
docs.text: Gemini vision rejects hard failures before a person sees an image, which shrinks the review pile. It can still be wrong, so auto_candidate assets are hidden from the app unless SHOW_AUTO_CANDIDATES=true. Approval is a deliberate human act.

docs.title: Failure Handling That Protects the Queue
docs.text: A job gets three attempts. A ComfyUI connection failure also breaks the worker loop, because otherwise one offline server would burn every job's retries in seconds. Deduplication refuses a job when an active one exists for the same asset, or when a usable asset is already in the catalogue.

docs.title: Generation Layer
docs.text:
• localComfyProvider.ts (422 lines) patches a workflow JSON template with prompt, seed and filenames, submits it to /prompt, polls /history/{id} and downloads the PNG
  • 9 workflow templates in workflows/comfy/ covering SDXL, SD1.5 and Flux Schnell variants
  • Input images reach ComfyUI by file copy into services/ComfyUI/input/

docs.title: Pipeline Layer
docs.text:
• generationWorker.ts resolves a pose control by frame_key or exercise name, fetches the persona master reference, generates, validates, then writes the catalogue entry
  • Vision parse failures and API errors are treated as reject, so a QA outage cannot let unchecked images through
  • Horizontal exercises get extra rubric rules, such as rejecting a standing figure

docs.title: Data and API Layer
docs.text:
• No database: three JSON files in src/data/ hold the assets, pose controls and jobs, plus exerciseLibrary.json for extracted content
  • 17 Next.js route handlers cover assets, jobs (cancel, retry, reject), pose controls, approval, master promotion and extraction

docs.title: Asset Lab UI
docs.text:
• /asset-lab is a 1,276-line page for job monitoring, candidate review and pose registration, with a 334-line canvas PoseGenerator.tsx
  • The route is internal tooling and must not be exposed publicly

docs.title: 📊 Key Metrics
docs.text:
• Source: 31 TypeScript files, 4,637 lines in src/
  • API routes: 17 route handlers
  • Workflow templates: 9 ComfyUI JSONs
  • Catalogue: 101 assets (98 female persona, 3 male), of which 6 approved, 92 auto_candidate and 3 human_rejected
  • Pose controls: 58 registered, 134 skeleton PNGs on disk
  • Jobs: 95 recorded, all ended as auto_candidate
  • Dependencies: 7 runtime, 8 dev (from package.json)

docs.title: 🛠️ Development Process
docs.text:
Built with Claude Code. The repo's CLAUDE.md records the hard-won rules: never accept an SD1.5 fallback, check the resolved model family before the prompt, and keep the Asset Lab private. Several one-off Node and Python scripts at the repo root (candidate generation, pose migration, OpenPose rendering) document the iteration that led to the queue-based pipeline. There are no automated tests, so quality control sits in the pipeline itself: vision QA plus human review.

This project demonstrates a practical generative-image pipeline with validation, human-in-the-loop review and local-first inference.

docs.title: Planning Replay — UK Planning Application Explorer
docs.text:
TL;DR: A map-based explorer for UK planning applications. Search by postcode or by map area, see what has been applied for nearby with a Now / Proposed / Completed view, layer in crime and facilities context, and place council plan PDFs on the map by hand-matching landmarks. It never invents buildings the source data doesn't support.

Stack: Python standard-library HTTP server • Vanilla JS + Leaflet • Planning Data API • UK PlanIt (fallback) • Overpass / data.police.uk • pypdf + pyproj • Node and Python tests

docs.title: ✨ Features
docs.text:
• 📮 Postcode or map search - Or explore the UK map and search around its centre, with 250 m, 500 m and 1 km radii
  • 🔄 Data fallback - The government Planning Data API is queried first; UK PlanIt is used when it returns nothing nearby
  • 🏘️ Neighbourhood scenarios - Now, Proposed and Completed views; Completed is only offered once a source site layout has been matched and located
  • 🗂️ Local filtering - Search loaded records by address, status or description; filters survive opening an application
  • 🗺️ Six on-demand overlays - Reported crime, schools, healthcare, parks, public transport, shops and community facilities, each fetched for the searched area
  • 📄 Council plan discovery - "Find plans" retrieves a Stafford application's document inventory and ranks site layouts and location plans first
  • 📐 Reviewed placement - Crop one drawing, match three landmarks, review the overlay, then save locally
  • 🧱 Optional OS context - Address points and street lines from OS open data, off by default
  • 🛡️ Bounded server - 15-minute caches, 40 MB document cap, timeouts on every upstream call

docs.title: Honesty about data
docs.text: Application points are approximate, not site boundaries, and an empty result is not proof that nothing exists. The app builds no future buildings or construction phases from them. Completed stays unavailable until a plan is matched and geolocated, and receipt dates are not treated as evidence that something was built. The Proposed view excludes refused, withdrawn and completed statuses but still doesn't claim construction is pending.

docs.title: Reviewed placement instead of automatic reconstruction
docs.text: Council registers differ, so the project ships one working connector (Stafford's Civica register) and a human-in-the-loop alignment step. The user matches three landmarks on drawing and map, and the app applies a three-point affine transform. It rejects collinear or mirrored matches and states that three points fit exactly and prove nothing about accuracy. The docs record that two real applications behaved differently and one council has no connector yet.

docs.title: Safe retrieval by construction
docs.text: The evidence API never fetches a caller-supplied URL. Document IDs must belong to the application's current inventory, downloads are capped at 40 MB, and preview subprocesses time out. Exact-reference matching rejects near-miss applications.

docs.title: Stale-work control in the UI
docs.text: The overlay controller keeps a generation counter and per-layer AbortControllers, so a new search cancels in-flight requests and discards late responses. Failed layers show a retry button, and "no records" is a different state from "source unavailable".

docs.title: Server
docs.text:
• server.py is a SimpleHTTPRequestHandler subclass exposing 11 API routes (720 lines)
  • neighbourhood.py validates layer, UK bounds and a 100 to 1000 m radius, then caches by key for 900 s with a 128 entry cap
  • Crime uses the latest reporting month from data.police.uk, filters to the search circle by haversine distance and groups incidents sharing a point

docs.title: Evidence pipeline
docs.text:
• planning_evidence.py classifies documents as location, layout, report or other from their titles
  • It scans PDF text for likely plan pages and explicit site-centre grid references, converting with pyproj
  • Inventories are cached 15 minutes and PDFs 24 hours, keyed by content hash

docs.title: Frontend
docs.text:
• Vendored Leaflet, no build step; scenario logic is split into small modules testable from Node
  • Saved placements are keyed to browser, application, PDF hash and page, and switching context removes the overlay

docs.text:
TL;DR: A fully client-side pitch demo that contrasts legacy PSTN banking support (dial, navigate a phone menu, wait, re-verify) with an AI-native, WebRTC-style in-app call. A 10-scene narrative plays in Today, Future or side-by-side Compare mode, with pre-generated British-English narration. It is a companion to the Ambient Banking Assistant.

docs.title: ✨ Features
docs.text:
• 🎬 10-scene narrative - Inbound support journey (scenes 0 to 7) followed by a secure outbound-call story (scenes 8 and 9), auto-advancing at 15 seconds per scene
  • ↔️ Three demo modes - Today, Future, and a synchronised Compare view that narrates each scene's delta
  • 📞 Session lifecycle - idle → connecting → active → handoff, derived from the current scene
  • 🧠 AI Context Drawer - Intent, confidence, signals and permitted actions for the moment on screen
  • 🛡️ Support policy engine - Eight named actions, each tagged none, low or medium risk, gated by intent and session state
  • 🤝 Human handoff package - A composed "context luggage" payload shown on a colleague desktop next to the customer phone
  • 🏗️ Architecture overlay - A strategic WebRTC vs PSTN diagram as scene 7
  • 🔊 Narration - 30 pre-generated MP3s (3 modes x 10 scenes) with a Web Speech API fallback
  • 🎛️ Presenter controls - Playback, speed, scene jump, narrator toggle, mode switch, reset
  • 🌗 Light and dark themes

    SE --> Ctx["DemoContext<br/>React Context"]
    SE --> Audio["Narration MP3s<br/>today / future / compare"]
    Ctx --> App["App.jsx<br/>scene to session state"]
    App --> Views["Mobile views<br/>Desktop handoff<br/>Architecture overlay"]

    idle --> connecting: scene 2
    connecting --> active: scenes 3 to 5

docs.title: Stable engines, no stale closures
docs.text: SceneEngine is a plain class created once via useRef. It holds the timer, current index, mode and speed outside React. Narration and scene-change callbacks reach React state through mutable refs (narratorEnabledRef, setCurrentSceneRef) that effects keep current. Auto-play therefore never reads stale state, and the engine is never re-created when the presenter flips a toggle mid-demo.

docs.title: Guardrails modelled, not just narrated
docs.text: The AI is shown acting inside a policy layer. supportIntentEngine maps a scene (and a flagged transaction) to an intent with a confidence score, for example 0.92 for a card dispute and 0.97 for escalation. supportPolicyEngine then returns only the actions allowed for that intent, and only View Transaction Detail while the session is idle or connecting. Both are commented as stand-ins for a real classifier and rules service.

docs.title: The handoff is the point
docs.text: Most chatbot demos end when the bot is done. Here, scene 6 renders the customer phone and a colleague desktop side by side, with a payload from handoffComposer: issue, transaction, actions taken, urgency, sentiment, recommended next step and a transcript excerpt. The specialist starts with context, which is the strongest contrast to a PSTN transfer where the customer repeats everything.

docs.title: Compare mode narrates the delta
docs.text: Compare narration is not today's script plus future's script. Each scene carries a delta line (for example "Anonymous PSTN number vs verified in-app identity") and a compareNarrative, and the compare MP3s speak that difference. This keeps side-by-side viewing short enough to follow.

docs.title: State and playback
docs.text:
• DemoContext exposes scene, mode, play state, speed, theme, narrator and drawer state through a useDemo() hook
  • Scene delay is (scene.duration || 15000) / speed; no scene sets its own duration, so all use 15 seconds scaled by the speed multiplier
  • App.jsx derives session state from the scene id in an effect, so the lifecycle always matches the scene the presenter jumps to

docs.title: Narration pipeline
docs.text:
• scripts/generate-narration-ssml.sh (348 lines) calls Amazon Polly (neural voice Amy, en-GB, 24 kHz) and writes public/narration/{mode}/scene{N}.mp3
  • Playback tries the MP3 first, and falls back to SpeechSynthesisUtterance only if that audio is still the active one, so TTS never overlaps a newer MP3

docs.title: UI and delivery
docs.text:
• MobileFrame (390x844) and DesktopFrame (1200x800) wrap views; Framer Motion handles scene transitions
  • Theme is applied by setting data-theme on the root element
  • A GitHub Actions workflow builds and deploys to GitHub Pages on push to main; narration paths use import.meta.env.BASE_URL so they work under a sub-path
