docs.title: IVR Evolution — From DTMF to AI Voice Agents
docs.text:
TL;DR: An interactive presentation demo that replays one scenario, a customer reporting a lost debit card, across five generations of phone banking. It runs from 2000s keypad menus to 2025 AI voice agents, then a speculative 2027+ era where the bank calls you. Each era is built to show what that technology could not do. There is no build step, framework or dependencies.

Stack: Vanilla JavaScript • Web Speech API • Web Audio API • WebSocket (optional live Nova Sonic backend) • Pre-recorded WAV clips

docs.title: ✨ Features
docs.text:
• 📞 Working DTMF keypad (2000s) - Real dual-tone sounds synthesised with Web Audio oscillators, navigating a menu tree that always ends in a hold queue
  • 🎙️ Deliberately flawed ASR (2010s) - Scripted playback with a 25% misrecognition chance and phrases like "cost card" and "ghost card", so the failure is visible
  • 🔊 Conversational bot (2020s) - Intent and slot-filling flow driven by 7 pre-recorded clips
  • 🤖 AI voice agent (2025) - Scripted playback from 9 clips, or a live WebSocket call to a Nova Sonic backend (see Voice S2S Platform)
  • 🎭 Off-script prompts - Five suggested interruptions in the 2025 era, such as "Can you just freeze everything on my account immediately?"
  • 📲 Proactive AI call (2027+) - Scripted branching flow where the AI phones the customer, backed by 7 clips
  • 🎬 Theater mode - Full-screen hardware render splash on each era switch, with pause and resume controls
  • ⌨️ Presenter keys - Left and right arrows move between eras, R resets the current era
  • ⚙️ Runtime settings - Override the WebSocket URL, AWS credentials and bank name without editing files
  • 📊 Per-era trade-off bars - Each era carries a trade-off position, tech badges and noise levels in config

docs.title: 🧠 Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    HTML["index.html<br/>sequential script tags"] --> Cfg["config.js<br/>CONFIG global"]
    Cfg --> Audio["AudioEngine<br/>window.audioEngine"]
    Cfg --> Main["main.js<br/>era controller"]
    Main -->|"new / destroy"| E0["Era2000"]
    Main --> E1["Era2010"]
    Main --> E2["Era2020"]
    Main --> E3["EraNow"]
    Main --> E4["Era2030"]
    E0 & E1 & E2 & E3 & E4 --> Audio
    Audio --> Out["DTMF, noise, ring tones,<br/>SpeechSynthesis, WAV files"]
    E3 -.->|"demoMode false"| WS["WebSocket<br/>Nova Sonic backend"]

The 2025 era has two paths. In demo mode it never touches the network. In live mode it streams microphone audio to the backend and plays the reply.

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as Presenter
    participant M as main.js
    participant E as EraNow
    participant B as Nova Sonic backend
    U->>M: Right arrow or era button
    M->>E: destroy previous era, init EraNow
    U->>E: Press call
    alt demoMode true
        E->>E: play scripted WAV clips
    else demoMode false
        E->>B: open WebSocket
        loop while connected
            E->>B: PCM16 16kHz mic frames
            B-->>E: PCM16 audio at 24kHz
        end
    end
    U->>E: End call

docs.title: Failure as the Product
docs.text: Each era is designed to show where its technology breaks. The 2000s menu tree routes the lost-card option to "cannot be completed via automated service" and then a 22-minute hold. The 2010s era injects misrecognition on 25% of turns from a fixed phrase list. Because the same scenario runs in every era, an audience compares the experiences directly instead of reading about them.

docs.title: Demo Mode Removes Live Risk
docs.text: Three eras ship with demoMode: true: 2010s, 2020s and 2025. Scripted playback means a presentation does not depend on microphone permission, room noise, or a network. Live recognition and the live Nova Sonic call remain one config flag away. The 2025 era can still go off-script with five prepared prompts when the presenter wants to show real behaviour.

docs.title: Config as Single Source of Truth
docs.text: config.js holds the bank name, backend settings, system prompt and per-era content: titles, badges, trade-off positions, menu trees, scripts and intent definitions. White-labelling for another bank means changing the bank name and the system prompt. The era classes contain behaviour only.

docs.title: Self-Contained Era Lifecycle
docs.text: Every era class implements init(container, convPanel) and destroy(). The controller creates one instance and tears it down on a switch, so each era starts clean when a presenter jumps back and forth mid-talk.

docs.title: Audio Layer
docs.text:
• AudioEngine is a single window.audioEngine instance shared by all eras
  • DTMF tones are generated from paired oscillators with short attack and release ramps to avoid clicks
  • Line noise and crackle come from a generated noise buffer, with levels set per era in config
  • Prompts use a pre-recorded file when one is configured and fall back to browser SpeechSynthesis otherwise

docs.title: Live Mode
docs.text:
• Microphone audio is sent as PCM16 mono, 16kHz, in 4096-sample chunks over binary WebSocket frames
  • Replies are played as PCM16 at 24kHz
  • If no AWS credentials are entered for a localhost backend, the UI shows a soft warning but still attempts the call, since the backend may hold credentials

docs.title: No-Build Delivery
docs.text:
• Scripts load in a fixed order from index.html: config, audio engine, five eras, then the controller
  • Shared ?v= query strings on every CSS and JS include handle cache-busting
  • Served with ./start.sh (Python http server on 8081) or npm start (npx serve on 8080); it must be served over HTTP, not file://
  • Speech recognition needs Chrome or Edge

docs.title: 📊 Key Metrics
docs.text:
• Eras: 5, all following one lost-card scenario
  • JavaScript: 3,317 lines across 7 files in js/, plus a 524-line config.js
  • CSS: 3,359 lines across 3 stylesheets
  • Audio clips: 23 WAV files (7 for 2020s, 9 for 2025, 7 for 2027+)
  • Hardware renders: 5 phone images, one per era
  • Dependencies: 0 runtime packages
  • Docs: A 138-line journey map documenting each era's flow

docs.title: 🔨 Development Process
docs.text:
Built with Claude Code as a small, single-purpose presentation tool. Clips are generated with three shell scripts using macOS say, so they can be regenerated when wording changes. The project's CLAUDE.md records the script load order, the era pattern and the cache-busting rule, so later edits stay consistent. The repo has 10 commits.

This project demonstrates how a deliberately simple, dependency-free build can make technology evolution tangible, by letting an audience feel each era's limits rather than read about them.

docs.title: demomcp — MCP Servers for Demo Recording
docs.text:
TL;DR: A monorepo of two Model Context Protocol servers that let an AI assistant record and publish demos. One captures a region of the macOS screen on the host, and the other runs inside Docker to turn the recording into an MP4, an optimised GIF, a poster frame and a ready-to-paste MkDocs snippet.

Stack: TypeScript • @modelcontextprotocol/sdk (stdio) • Zod • ffmpeg + AVFoundation • gifsicle • AppleScript • Docker (node:20-alpine)

docs.title: ✨ Features
docs.text:
• 🎥 screen-recorder-host - Host-side MCP server with 5 tools: list_devices, position_chrome, start_recording, stop_recording and status
  • 🪟 Window staging - position_chrome drives Google Chrome through AppleScript so every recording starts from the same frame (defaults to 1280x720 at 0,80)
  • ✂️ Region capture - ffmpeg and AVFoundation record a cropped region at a configurable frame rate (default 30 fps), with an optional duration cap
  • 🐳 demo-recorder-docker - Containerised MCP server with 6 tools: convert_video, gifify, optimize_gif, publish_assets, mkdocs_snippet and convert_and_publish
  • 🎞️ Two-pass GIFs - ffmpeg palettegen then paletteuse with a selectable dither (none, sierra2_4a, bayer), followed by gifsicle -O3
  • 📦 Asset publishing - Copies outputs into docs/assets/demos/<slug>/ and extracts a poster JPG at the 1-second mark
  • 📝 MkDocs snippets - Emits a <video> embed with poster and GIF fallback, or a GIF-only <figure> when preferGif is set
  • 🧰 Typed tools - Every tool has a Zod input schema with defaults and returns both text and structuredContent
  • ⚡ One-shot mode - MCP_ONESHOT=1 with ARGS_JSON runs the whole pipeline as a plain CLI, bypassing MCP for quick testing

docs.title: 🧠 Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    AI["AI assistant<br/>MCP client"] -->|stdio| Rec["screen-recorder-host<br/>native macOS process"]
    Rec -->|spawn| FF["ffmpeg<br/>avfoundation"]
    Rec -->|osascript| Chrome["Google Chrome<br/>window bounds"]
    FF --> Raw["Raw MP4 in /tmp"]

    AI -->|stdio via docker run| Proc["demo-recorder-docker<br/>node:20-alpine"]
    Raw -->|"mounted /tmp"| Proc
    Proc --> FF2["ffmpeg + gifsicle"]
    FF2 --> Assets["docs/assets/demos/slug<br/>demo.mp4, demo.gif, poster.jpg"]
    Proc --> Snip["MkDocs HTML snippet"]
    Assets --> Site["MkDocs site"]
    Snip --> Site

The two servers never talk to each other. The assistant hands the recording path from one to the other, and the shared /tmp mount is what makes that path valid on both sides.

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as AI assistant
    participant H as screen-recorder-host
    participant D as demo-recorder-docker
    A->>H: position_chrome
    A->>H: start_recording
    H-->>A: outPath in /tmp
    Note over A,H: demo is performed
    A->>H: stop_recording
    H-->>A: finalised MP4 path
    A->>D: convert_and_publish with inputPath and slug
    D->>D: convert, gifify, optimize, publish, poster
    D-->>A: outDir, outMp4, outGif, poster, snippet

docs.title: Split by Trust Boundary
docs.text: Screen capture needs AVFoundation, AppleScript and macOS permissions, so it cannot live in a container and runs natively. Video processing needs a specific ffmpeg and gifsicle toolchain, so it is the opposite: pinned inside an Alpine image where it behaves identically on any machine. The split puts each server where its dependencies already are, and the bin/ wrappers hide the difference from the client.

docs.title: Closes the Loop to Publication
docs.text: Most recording tools stop at a video file. convert_and_publish carries on: it places assets at the path MkDocs expects, makes a poster, and returns the HTML to paste. Recording a demo and getting it onto a page becomes one conversation instead of a manual ffmpeg session.

docs.title: Granular Tools Plus an Orchestrator
docs.text: The pipeline is exposed twice. The individual tools (convert_video, gifify, optimize_gif, publish_assets) let an assistant redo one step, for example re-running the GIF at a different dither without re-encoding. convert_and_publish runs the full chain in one call when the defaults are fine. Both share the same Zod defaults, so behaviour stays consistent.

docs.title: A Non-MCP Escape Hatch
docs.text: MCP_ONESHOT=1 makes the same server run the pipeline from an ARGS_JSON environment variable and exit with JSON on stdout. That allows the container to be tested from a shell, or in a script, without an MCP client attached.

docs.title: Host Recorder
docs.text:
• A single module-level active record holds the ffmpeg child process, so only one recording can run at a time. A second start_recording returns the existing path instead of starting another
  • stop_recording sends SIGINT and waits for the process close event, which lets ffmpeg write the MP4 trailer so the file is playable
  • position_chrome writes a temporary AppleScript to /tmp and passes the geometry as argv, rather than interpolating values into script text

docs.title: Processing Container
docs.text:
• All subprocess calls go through one run() wrapper around execFile with a 10 MB buffer; failures reject with ffmpeg's stderr, so the assistant sees the real error
  • Encoding uses H.264 libx264, veryfast preset, yuv420p for broad playback compatibility, lanczos scaling with an even height (scale=W:-2) and audio stripped
  • crf is bounded to 18-35 and GIF colours to 32-256 by the schemas, so out-of-range values are rejected before ffmpeg runs

docs.title: Packaging
docs.text:
• npm workspaces monorepo; both packages use the same dependency ranges (@modelcontextprotocol/sdk ^1.20.0, zod ^3.23.8, TypeScript ^5.6.3)
  • The root run:docker:oneshot script mounts $PWD as /repo and /tmp as /tmp so inputs and published assets land on the host

docs.title: 📊 Key Metrics
docs.text:
• MCP tools: 11 in total (5 host, 6 container)
  • Source size: 538 lines of TypeScript across the two entry files (135 host, 403 container)
  • Packages: 2 in an npm workspace, both on @modelcontextprotocol/sdk ^1.20.0
  • Runtime dependencies: 2 per package (MCP SDK and Zod)
  • Container: node:20-alpine with ffmpeg and gifsicle from apk
  • Steering docs: 3 (product.md, structure.md, tech.md under .kiro/steering/)
  • Automated tests: none; the one-shot mode is the manual smoke test

docs.text:
Developed with Claude Code (the repo carries a CLAUDE.md) and Kiro steering documents describing the product, structure and tech choices. The repository has 6 commits.

This project demonstrates building practical MCP tooling that automates a real workflow, from window positioning to a published, embeddable demo.

docs.title: Agent-Driven UI — No Hardcoded Screens
docs.text: Most voice assistants return text. This one returns a component tree. The LangGraph agent emits server.a2ui.patch messages containing a flat list of typed components with parent–child references. A2Renderer.tsx builds the tree at runtime and renders it. Add a new component type on the server; the client renders it automatically. Remove a screen; the agent simply stops emitting it.

docs.title: Single Outbox, Coordinated Delivery
docs.text: The agent queues all output — UI patches, voice lines, transcripts — into a state.outbox. process_outbox() always flushes non-voice events first, then batches all speech into a single TTS call. This prevents audio from playing before the UI has updated.

docs.title: Trouble-Aware Conversation
docs.text: The agent tracks trouble_count: how many turns the user gave no useful information or used struggle keywords. At ≥ 2, show_support flips to true and the frontend surfaces a human escalation button — all without any client-side logic changes.

docs.title: LangGraph State Machine
docs.text:
• Nodes: ingest_input, interpret_intent, render_missing_inputs, call_mortgage_tools, render_products_a2ui, handle_ui_action, recalculate_and_patch, render_summary_a2ui, confirm_application, clear_pending_action
  • State: Single AgentState object as source of truth — intent, ltv, products, selection, ui, outbox, trouble_count
  • Routing: start_router dispatches on message type (transcript vs UI action); intent_router branches on field completeness

docs.title: Amazon Nova Sonic Integration
docs.text:
• STT: Node.js subprocess (nova_sonic_stt.mjs) receiving PCM16 via stdin, emitting TRANSCRIPT: lines on stdout
  • TTS: Separate Node.js subprocess (nova_sonic_tts.mjs) emitting AUDIO_CHUNK:<base64> lines, forwarded as WebSocket binary frames
  • Fallback: Keyword-based intent extraction when AWS is unavailable

docs.title: Client Audio Pipeline
docs.text:
• AudioWorkletNode (PCM16Processor) records at 16 kHz; chunks base64-encoded to server
  • VAD: auto-stops after 1500 ms silence below 0.015 RMS
  • AudioStreamer queues base64 PCM16 chunks on a 24 kHz AudioContext; mic auto-restarts after TTS playback ends

docs.title: A2UI Component Library
docs.text: Supported types: Column, Row, Text (h1/h2/h3/body), Gauge, ProductCard, Button, Map (Leaflet iframe), Timeline, DataCard, BenefitCard, ComparisonBadge, Image. Unknown types render as a visible error box — no silent failures.

  • Test coverage: Goal-based integration tests for full conversation scenarios (e.g. GBT-FTB-01 first-time buyer flow)
  • UI components: 13 dynamic component types, zero hardcoded screens
  • Models used: Amazon Nova Sonic (voice), Amazon Nova Lite (intent/guardrails), Claude Sonnet/Haiku (A2UI design)

docs.title: Phantom Action Watcher
docs.text: LLMs frequently say "I'll check your balance now" and then return a text response instead of calling the tool. phantom-action-watcher.ts monitors every turn for high-confidence verbal commitments (balance check, transaction lookup, dispute filing) and, if no corresponding tool call appears in the same response, issues a silent reprompt. Users never see the failure; the model self-corrects.

docs.title: Dual Brain, One Interface
docs.text: The same frontend, same WebSocket protocol, and same tool definitions work across both brain modes. Nova Sonic Direct runs tools natively within the model stream for minimal latency. Bedrock Agent mode hands off to AWS AgentCore for complex multi-step reasoning. Switching modes is a runtime setting — no redeployment.

docs.title: Tool System as Configuration
docs.text: Every tool is a JSON file: name, description, input_schema, instruction, category, optional gatewayTarget. Setting gatewayTarget routes the call through AgentCoreGatewayClient using AWS SigV4-signed MCP requests. Tools without gatewayTarget run locally. Adding a capability is dropping a file — no TypeScript changes.

docs.title: Dialect-Aware Conversations
docs.text: AWS Transcribe Streaming returns language identification confidence scores alongside transcripts. dialect-detector.ts maps locale codes (en-GB, fr-FR, etc.) to voice IDs. When confidence crosses a threshold, transition-handler.ts calls Bedrock to generate a natural "let me switch to your language" phrase, then swaps the active voice mid-session.

docs.title: AI Governance Unit (AIGU) — Continuous AI Governance Orchestration
docs.text:
TL;DR: A 9-agent LangGraph system that replaces manual AI governance checklists with a continuous orchestration loop. Projects flow through a structured lifecycle — Intake → Risk → POC → Pilot → Librarian → Gatekeeper → Production → Handover — with specialized Amazon Nova agents handling each stage, automatic delta detection, and a universal support overlay at every step.

Stack: Python • LangGraph • Amazon Nova (Pro/Lite) • AWS Bedrock • AWS Lambda • DynamoDB • S3 • React Native • Expo • LangFuse

docs.title: ✨ Features
docs.text:
• 🧠 9-Agent Brain - Each lifecycle stage has a dedicated agent with focused responsibilities; no monolithic prompt
  • ⚡ Dual Paths - Hero capabilities fast-track through an Accelerator path (skip POC); New capabilities follow the full Standard path with CAF approval
  • 📊 15% Delta Threshold - Production changes are auto-analysed; updates exceeding 15% trigger full GIGC re-approval automatically
  • 🔄 State-Loop Architecture - React Native frontend is a "dumb" terminal; all state lives in DynamoDB, managed by LangGraph
  • 🛡️ Universal Support Overlay - A read-only Support & Insights agent is available at every stage for status queries and "why" explanations
  • 📋 Artifact Management - Governance Librarian validates required artifacts by risk level and prevents duplication via automated audits
  • 🔍 LangFuse Tracing - Full prompt management and observability across all agent invocations
  • 🧪 TDD Lifecycle Simulations - Pytest-driven end-to-end lifecycle tests covering all paths and edge cases

docs.title: Governance as a State Machine, Not a Spreadsheet
docs.text: Traditional AI governance is checklists, email chains, and manual sign-offs. AIGU models the entire lifecycle as a LangGraph state machine. Every transition — approval, rejection, delta re-review — is a graph edge. Stage-specific agents run in sequence; the Support agent is always available as a side channel. The governance process becomes auditable, automatable, and queryable.

docs.title: Delta-Driven Re-Approval
docs.text: When a production AI system changes, most governance processes require a full manual re-review by default. AIGU's Production agent computes the delta between the current and prior submission. Changes under 15% proceed without re-approval; changes over 15% automatically re-route through the Gatekeeper. The threshold is configurable and the logic is transparent.

docs.title: Hero vs. New Paths
docs.text: Not all AI capabilities need the same scrutiny. "Hero" capabilities (proven patterns within existing guardrails) skip the POC stage entirely and fast-track to Pilot. "New" capabilities follow the full Standard path including CAF approval. The Intake agent classifies the path from the initial submission; humans only intervene at defined gates.

docs.title: LangGraph Orchestration
docs.text:
• State machine: aigu/graph.py — a compiled LangGraph graph with conditional edges for path routing
  • State persistence: DynamoDB-backed LangGraph checkpoints for resumable sessions
  • Agent dispatch: each agent in aigu/agents/ receives the full state, acts on its slice, and returns a patch

docs.title: Amazon Nova via Bedrock
docs.text:
• Nova Pro: used for high-stakes decisions (risk classification, gatekeeper review, production delta analysis)
  • Nova Lite: used for lower-stakes parsing (intake extraction, librarian checks, support queries)
  • LangFuse: all prompts versioned and served at runtime; traces every invocation for debugging

docs.text:

docs.title: MyStaycation — UK Holiday Price Watcher
docs.text:
TL;DR: A personal price-monitoring assistant for UK staycations (Hoseasons and Haven). It builds a price history over time, compares current prices against that history, and emails you only when a booking is genuinely worth acting on — not just because a price changed.

Stack: Node.js • TypeScript • Fastify • PostgreSQL • TypeORM • Redis • BullMQ • Next.js • Playwright • Docker Compose • AWS SES • Nginx

docs.title: ✨ Features
docs.text:
• 📈 Historical Price Tracking - Stores price snapshots over time to establish a real baseline; alerts are anchored to history, not absolute price
  • 🎯 Smart Alert Thresholds - Configurable conditions for what counts as a meaningful deal; avoids noise from minor fluctuations
  • 🌐 Browser-Based Scraping - Playwright handles providers that require JavaScript rendering (Hoseasons, Haven)
  • ⚙️ Kill Switches - Per-provider and global scraping toggles via environment variables; no code changes needed to pause a provider
  • 📧 Email Notifications - AWS SES integration with fallback to SMTP; email verification required before alerts are sent
  • 🔐 Secure Authentication - JWT with email verification and password reset; bcrypt password hashing
  • 🐳 Dev + Prod Profiles - Single Docker Compose file with separate dev and prod profiles; Nginx proxy in production

docs.title: History-Anchored Alerts
docs.text: Most price trackers alert on any drop. This one builds a historical baseline per holiday and only alerts when a price is meaningfully below what it's typically been — accounting for seasonal patterns. You get notified when a deal is actually unusual, not just when a provider tweaks a price by £5.

docs.title: Kill Switches Without Deployments
docs.text: Providers change their sites without warning. Rather than requiring a code fix and redeployment to pause a broken scraper, the system reads environment variables at job dispatch time. PROVIDER_HOSEASONS_ENABLED=false stops Hoseasons jobs immediately. SCRAPING_ENABLED=false stops everything. No restarts required.

docs.title: Respectful Scraping
docs.text:
• Runs at 24–72 hour intervals to avoid hammering providers
  • Identifies itself with descriptive User-Agent headers
  • Respects robots.txt
  • Full audit log of every fetch operation

docs.title: Backend (Fastify + TypeScript)
docs.text:
• Queue architecture: Redis + BullMQ handles all scraping as background jobs with retry logic and concurrency controls
  • TypeORM: entity-based schema management with migrations; PostgreSQL for all persistent data
  • Playwright concurrency: PLAYWRIGHT_CONCURRENCY env var caps browser instances to manage memory in constrained environments

docs.title: Frontend (Next.js)
docs.text:
• Responsive design — accessible on mobile for on-the-go deal checking
  • Holiday profile management: set preferences once, monitor continuously

docs.title: Infrastructure
docs.text:
• Dev profile: direct port exposure (:3000 frontend, :4000 API), no Nginx
  • Prod profile: Nginx reverse proxy with rate limiting and security headers
  • docker-compose exec api npm run seed to populate initial provider and configuration data
  • AWS SES for production email; console log fallback for local development

docs.title: 📊 Key Metrics
docs.text:
• Providers: Hoseasons, Haven (extensible via provider guide in docs/development/PROVIDER_GUIDE.md)
  • Scrape interval: 24–72 hours (configurable per provider)
  • Alert logic: threshold-based against historical price baseline
  • Auth: JWT + bcrypt + email verification + password reset

A practical full-stack project solving a real personal need: monitoring holiday prices intelligently so you only have to act when it actually matters.
